  2. Most side effects are mild and ease with time. They tend to show up early and after a dose increase.
  3. Serious side effects are far less common. Know the warning signs, such as severe stomach pain or sudden vision changes.
  4. Some people should not take it. A personal or family history of certain thyroid cancers is the main reason.

Semaglutide is one of the most widely used GLP-1 medicines for type 2 diabetes and weight management. Like every medicine, it can cause side effects, and knowing which ones are normal and which ones need a doctor makes treatment safer.

In most cases, the side effects are digestive and short-lived. Below, we explain the common ones, how long they usually last, what helps, the serious risks to watch for, and who should not take semaglutide or tirzepatide.

Most Common Semaglutide Side Effects

Most semaglutide side effects affect the stomach and gut. The rates below come from the US label for Wegovy, the weight-management brand, compared with placebo.

Side effect How common (vs placebo) What it can feel like What can help
Nausea 44% vs 16% Feeling queasy or off your food, often after eating Eat slowly, have smaller meals, stop when you feel satisfied, and avoid fatty, fried or spicy food
Diarrhoea 30% vs 16% Loose or more frequent stools Sip clear fluids and cut back on dairy, coffee and alcohol for a while
Vomiting 24% vs 6% Being sick, usually alongside nausea Take small sips of fluid and avoid lying down soon after eating
Constipation 24% vs 11% Harder or less frequent stools Add fibre, drink 2 to 3 litres of fluid a day and stay active
Abdominal pain 20% vs 10% Cramping or discomfort in the stomach Choose smaller meals; get urgent help if the pain is severe and does not go away
Headache 14% vs 10% Mild to moderate head pain Drink enough fluids and speak to a pharmacist if it keeps coming back
Tiredness 11% vs 5% Low energy during the day Keep to three regular meals with protein and fibre
Dizziness 8% vs 4% Feeling light-headed Do not drive or use machinery until it passes

The rates are lower in people taking semaglutide for type 2 diabetes. On the Ozempic label, nausea affected 15.8% to 20.3% of people, compared with 6.1% on placebo, because those trials used lower doses.

The NHS also lists hair loss, and itchy or red skin where you inject, among the common side effects. Overall, only a minority of people stop: in the Wegovy trials, 6.8% stopped because of side effects, compared with 3.2% on placebo.

How Long Do Semaglutide Side Effects Last?

For most people, the stomach side effects are strongest in the first weeks and after each dose increase. NHS guidance describes them as common, adding that they usually decrease over time as the body gets used to the medicine.

That is why both US labels start semaglutide at a low dose and raise it step by step over several weeks. This “start low, go slow” approach gives your gut time to adjust. If a dose is hard to tolerate, the Wegovy label lets your doctor wait longer before the next increase.

If side effects bother you or do not go away, speak to your doctor or pharmacist. The NHS advises keeping taking your medicine unless you are told to stop.

Why Does Semaglutide Cause Stomach Side Effects?

The stomach effects come from the same action that makes semaglutide work. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist, which means it copies GLP-1, a hormone your gut releases after meals.

Slower Stomach Emptying

GLP-1 slows the rate at which food leaves your stomach. You feel full for longer, but the same effect can bring on nausea, bloating, indigestion and vomiting. We explain how semaglutide works in more detail in a separate guide.

Appetite Signals in the Brain

GLP-1 also acts on the parts of the brain that control appetite, so you eat less. Together with slower digestion, this changes how your gut handles food, which is why both diarrhoea and constipation are more common than with placebo.

Who Is More Likely to Get Semaglutide Side Effects?

Anyone can get side effects, but some situations make them more likely or more serious. Based on the US labels, these include:

  • Higher doses. Rates were much higher at the weight-management dose (Wegovy) than in the diabetes trials (Ozempic).
  • The weeks after a dose increase. This is when the gut is still adjusting to the new dose.
  • Taking insulin or a sulfonylurea. Combining these with semaglutide raises the risk of low blood sugar.
  • Existing diabetic eye disease. In one two-year trial, eye complications rose more in people who already had diabetic retinopathy.
  • Very slow stomach emptying. The Ozempic label does not recommend semaglutide for people with severe gastroparesis.
  • Rapid weight loss. Losing weight quickly is linked to gallstones.

How Can You Reduce Semaglutide Side Effects?

Small changes to how you eat and drink often make a real difference. Alongside the tips in the table above, NHS guidance suggests:

  • Let your doctor set the pace. Do not raise the dose faster than prescribed.
  • Go easy on alcohol. The NHS notes that alcohol can make nausea and vomiting worse.
  • Use a smaller plate. Eat slowly and stop as soon as you feel full.
  • Keep a short food diary. Noting meals and timings can help you spot what triggers symptoms.
  • Drink plenty of fluids. Drink more if you have vomiting or diarrhoea, to avoid dehydration.
  • Speak up early. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about side effects that bother you or do not go away, rather than stopping on your own.

What Are the Serious Side Effects of Semaglutide?

Serious side effects are far less common than stomach upset. The NHS describes them as rare. Still, they need prompt attention, so it helps to know what they look like. The points below come from the US labels for Wegovy (revised October 2025) and Ozempic.

Thyroid C-Cell Tumour Warning

This is the label’s boxed warning. Semaglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents, and it is not known whether this happens in humans. Report a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, shortness of breath or hoarseness that does not go away.

Pancreatitis

Inflammation of the pancreas usually shows up as severe stomach pain that does not go away and may spread to your back, sometimes with vomiting. Stop semaglutide and seek medical help if this happens.

Gallbladder Problems

Gallstones and gallbladder inflammation have been reported, especially with rapid weight loss. Watch for pain in the upper right side of your stomach, fever, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

Kidney Problems From Dehydration

Repeated vomiting or diarrhoea can dehydrate you enough to strain your kidneys. In rare post-marketing cases, people needed dialysis. Keeping your fluids up during a stomach upset helps prevent this.

Low Blood Sugar

The risk is mainly in people who also take insulin or a sulfonylurea. Signs include sweating, shaking, a pounding heartbeat and dizziness.

Eye Problems

In people with type 2 diabetes, diabetic retinopathy complications were slightly more common on semaglutide (3% versus 1.8% in a two-year trial). Separately, the European Medicines Agency concluded in June 2025 that sudden vision loss from an optic nerve condition called NAION is a very rare side effect, affecting up to 1 in 10,000 people.

Other Label Warnings

The labels also warn about serious allergic reactions, a faster heart rate, and a risk of inhaling stomach contents under general anaesthesia or deep sedation. The Wegovy label adds monitoring for low mood or suicidal thoughts. Always tell your doctor or dentist that you take semaglutide before a procedure.

Who Should Not Take Semaglutide or Tirzepatide?

Semaglutide and tirzepatide share most of their safety rules. Semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy) acts on the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound) acts on the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and we cover how tirzepatide works in its own guide. The points below come from the US labels for Wegovy and Mounjaro.

People With a Personal or Family History of Thyroid Cancer

You should not use either drug if you or a close family member has had medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), an inherited condition linked to this cancer.

People With a Serious Allergy to the Drug

If you have had a serious allergic reaction to semaglutide, tirzepatide or any ingredient in the product, you should not use it again.

People Who Are Pregnant or Planning a Pregnancy

The Wegovy label advises stopping semaglutide at least two months before a planned pregnancy. With tirzepatide, tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to be. Tirzepatide can also make birth control pills less reliable, so its label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

People Who Need Extra Caution

Some conditions do not rule the drugs out but call for a careful talk with your doctor first: a past episode of pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney problems, diabetic retinopathy or severe gastroparesis. If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, your doctor may need to adjust those doses.

When Should You Call a Doctor?

Mild nausea in the first weeks is normal and usually settles. These signs are different. Seek medical attention if you notice:

  • Severe abdominal pain that does not go away, sometimes spreading to the back, with or without vomiting
  • Pain in the upper right abdomen, fever, or yellowing of the skin or eyes
  • A lump or swelling in the neck, trouble swallowing, or hoarseness that does not go away
  • Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or a severe rash
  • Vomiting or diarrhoea that will not stop, or passing much less urine than usual
  • A sudden change in vision, or loss of vision in one eye
  • Shakiness, sweating, confusion or a fast heartbeat if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea
  • New or worse depression, or thoughts of self-harm

Trouble breathing or a swollen throat is an emergency, so get urgent care straight away. For the other signs, contact the doctor who prescribed semaglutide before your next dose. If you feel dizzy or your vision changes, the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using machinery until it passes.

Is Semaglutide Available in Indonesia?

Yes. Semaglutide is registered with BPOM as a prescription medicine, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for weight management. A doctor prescribes it after reviewing your health history, including the conditions listed above, and a licensed pharmacy dispenses it.

Semaglutide is also available in Bali as a research compound, supplied for laboratory and research use and sometimes sold as “sema” or “GLP-1 SMA”. If you are buying for research, you can check our semaglutide prices in Bali. Our semaglutide is sold for research use only. It is not Ozempic, Wegovy or Rybelsus, it is not a BPOM-registered medicine, and it is not approved for human use.

Conclusion

Most semaglutide side effects are digestive, mild and short-lived. Nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation are the most common, especially in the first weeks and after a dose increase, and they usually ease as your body adjusts. Starting low, going slow, eating smaller meals and staying hydrated all help.

Serious side effects are far less common, but you should know the warning signs: severe stomach pain, a lump in your neck, swelling of your face or throat, or a sudden change in vision. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are not for anyone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2, and both need care around pregnancy.

In Indonesia, semaglutide is available on prescription as Ozempic and Wegovy, and in Bali as a research compound supplied for research use only.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Semaglutide Nausea Go Away?

Usually, yes. Nausea is most common in the first weeks and after each dose increase, and it tends to ease as your body adjusts. Tell your doctor if it does not improve.

Can Semaglutide Cause Thyroid Cancer?

It is not known. Semaglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents, which is why the label carries a boxed warning and rules it out for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2.

Does Semaglutide Cause Low Blood Sugar?

Not often on its own. The risk increases when semaglutide is taken with insulin or a sulfonylurea, so your doctor may lower those doses.

Can Semaglutide Affect Your Eyes?

In rare cases, yes. People with diabetic eye disease can see it worsen, and a sudden optic nerve problem called NAION is a very rare side effect. Report any change in vision.

Does Semaglutide Cause Hair Loss?

It can. The NHS lists hair loss among the common side effects of semaglutide.

When Should I Get Urgent Help?

Get urgent help for trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or severe stomach pain that does not go away. These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction or pancreatitis.

Do I Need to Stop Semaglutide Before Surgery?

Tell your surgeon, anaesthetist or dentist that you take it. The label warns about a risk of inhaling stomach contents under general anaesthesia or deep sedation, and your care team will decide what to do.

Are Ozempic and Wegovy Side Effects the Same?

Yes, the types are the same because both contain semaglutide. They are more frequent with Wegovy, which goes up to a higher dose.

What Does “Efek Samping Semaglutide” Mean?

It is Indonesian for “semaglutide side effects”. The answer is the same: mainly nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation, plus the rarer serious warnings above.
